newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexicans vote in strife-torn state, brace for trouble.
newsitem.headline: Mexicans vote in strife-torn state, brace for trouble.

text.p: Mexicans voted on Sunday in the strife-torn southwestern state of Guerrero amid fears that a contested result in the local poll could lead to violence between the strong-arm government and an angry opposition.

Many were braced for trouble following a recent surge in political violence, but there were only isolated reports of trouble during the vote to elect new mayors and a new state congress. Results were not expected until later in the night.

Keeping to the sidelines were thousands of army troops and armed rebels of the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR), a group which first appeared in this state and could use a contested election as an excuse to launch new attacks against the army.

Although army troops were ordered to suspend counter-insurgency operations against the EPR and return to their barracks for the day, groups of state police armed with automatic weapons roamed the streets in most cities across the state. Observers said poor voter turnout may have been due to fear of violence.

An electoral observer of the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) was stabbed to death early on Sunday in the town of Altamirano, some 150 miles (260 km) north of the state capital Chilpancingo.
State Attorney General Antonio Hernandez Diaz said he believed the incident was not related to the elections.

Shaved voter lists, vote buying and other irregularities were reported in different parts of the state, according to a Mexican electoral watchdog known as Alianza Civica, which had some 300 observers across the state.

In the town of Xochipala, some 50 kilometres (35 miles) south of Chilpancingo, heated arguments flared when a local PRI leader and head of the town's voting station turned up drunk and did not want PRD members to help count ballots.

"It's always the same thing. The PRI wins no matter what happens. I think people are getting tired of this," said Florencio Garcia Martinez, a 48-year-old construction worker in the nearby town of Zumpango.
Luciano Perez, an elementary school teacher in Zumpango, said people in his neighbourhood were offered free bags of cement if they could prove they voted for PRI candidates.

Across Mexico, the election was being closely watched following a wave of violence between local members of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) and the mostly leftist PRD that has killed 120 people in the past year.
PRD leaders have vowed to contest any outcome they consider the product of fraud and had already complained that the PRI used dirty pre-electoral tactics to gain votes.

The PRI was expected to win nearly all the races, including the state capital Chilpancingo and the posh tourist resort of Acapulco, despite an economic crisis and a series of political scandals that have cost it support across Mexico.
The PRI, which has ruled Mexico for 67 consecutive years, has overwhelming political power in the state, controlling 68 of the 76 town halls. The leftist PRD runs six towns.

PRI banners, swathed in the colours of the Mexican flag, festooned the streets of Chilpancingo over the weekend. The advertisements reminded voters of the EPR's deadly tactics in the state by featuring a giant dove next to the slogan: "Vote for peace, vote for unity."
